items.title: Related party under IBC- A paradox for financial creditors
items.summary: On October 27, 2026, the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, in the matter of ECL Finance Ltd. v. Abhinav Mukherjee (Civil Appeal No. 6268 of 2022) held that an institutional lender (also being a debenture holder) was a "related party" of the corporate debtor under Section 5(24)(m)(i) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC). Both the lender as well its debenture trustee by implication, were therefore barred from the Committee of Creditors (CoC). The lender was not a promoter or a promoter's proxy. It was excluded because of the covenants mentioned in the debenture trust deed and other loan documents to protect the interest of the lender and secure repayment of its money. The first principle The IBC is not a recovery statute. Swiss Ribbons described it as "a beneficial legislation which puts the corporate debtor back on its feet, not being a mere recovery legislation for creditors." But IBC chose a specific means of achieving revival: a CoC of financial creditors. They were chosen because, in Swiss Ribbons' words, they are "from the very beginning, involved with assessing the viability of the corporate debtor." The related-party exclusion protects that body.
